title: Rolling Ball Stops on the Mark
statement:
A ball sits in a grid maze, where 0 is an open cell and 1 is a wall. Everything outside the grid also counts as wall.

The ball starts at rest on cell start = [row, col]. You can push it up, down, left or right. Once pushed, it keeps rolling in that direction until the next cell is a wall, and only then stops. While it rolls you cannot steer it. After it stops you may push it again in any direction.

Return true if the ball can come to rest exactly on cell target. Rolling over the target without stopping there does not count. If target equals start, the ball is already resting there, so the answer is true.

examples.why: Push right: the wall at (0, 2) stops the ball at (0, 1). Push down: it rolls to the bottom edge at (3, 1). Push right: it stops against the edge at (3, 3).
The ball rolls across (1, 1) on several routes, but nothing next to it can stop it there. A normal "reachable cell" search would wrongly say true.
Pushed right, the ball passes (0, 1) and stops only at the edge, (0, 2).

constraints: start and target are open cells
hints: The interesting positions are not cells the ball passes but cells where it stops. Think of those as the nodes of a graph.
From a resting cell there are at most four moves. Simulate each roll until the next cell is a wall; the cell it ends on is a neighbour in the graph.
Run BFS or DFS over resting cells with a visited set, and answer true as soon as a roll stops on the target.

explain.intuition:
Forget the cells the ball merely rolls over. What matters is where it can rest, because only there can you choose a new direction. Each resting cell has up to four neighbours: the cells where the four rolls end. That is an ordinary graph, just with long edges.

So run a normal graph search over resting cells. To find a neighbour, simulate the roll step by step until the next cell is a wall or the edge. Mark resting cells as visited, not every cell passed, otherwise you would block valid stops that you merely rolled across earlier.
steps: Put start in a queue and mark it visited.
Pop a resting cell. If it is target, return true.
For each of the four directions, move one step at a time while the next cell is inside the grid and open.
The cell where the roll ends is a new resting cell. If it is not visited, mark it and add it to the queue.
pitfalls: Treating every cell the ball passes as reachable. The second example rolls over the target without ever stopping there.
Marking passed-over cells as visited, which can hide a real stop at that cell from another direction.
Rolling one step too far: stop when the next cell is blocked, not when the current one is.

complexity.time: O(rows · cols · (rows + cols)): each resting cell is expanded once and each roll is at most a full row or column

solutions.title: DFS over resting cells
solutions.idea: Recurse from each resting cell into the four cells where the rolls end, skipping cells already visited.

solutions.title: BFS over resting cells
solutions.idea: Same graph, explored level by level. BFS also gives the fewest pushes if you need that later.

followups: Return the shortest total distance rolled to stop on the target. Why does plain BFS no longer work, and what replaces it?
Precompute, for every cell and direction, where a roll from it ends. How does that change the cost per search?
